analysis.one_liner: Creates ethics-advisory and investigative offices inside the Supreme Court to police justices' gifts and conflicts.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on its introduction day and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended; no Republican cosponsored it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up two new offices inside the Supreme Court. One would give justices official lawyers to consult about gifts, financial disclosures, and conflicts of interest. The other would investigate ethics complaints against justices, with power to subpoena witnesses and documents, and would report findings to the Chief Justice — or, if the complaint is about the Chief Justice, to the most senior other justice. Under current rules the Supreme Court polices itself; this would put staff, paperwork, and real investigation behind that process.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who wants to know whether the nine justices with life tenure and final say on federal law are following the same ethics rules that bind other federal judges and officials. Litigants before the Court, and members of Congress who now have no way to act on ethics complaints against a justice, would gain an official channel.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Court watchers, litigants, and oversight-minded citizens

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Office of Ethics Counsel within the Supreme Court to advise justices and their spouses on financial disclosures, gifts, political activity, conflicts and recusal, with required biannual ethics training for every justice [S2].
Creates an Office of Investigative Counsel that can investigate ethics complaints against justices, with subpoena power enforceable through federal court and contempt penalties [S2].
Requires an annual report to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees on how often ethics advice was sought, what topics came up, and how often justices did not follow it [S2].
Investigation reports must be delivered to four congressional committees, and the office must refer reasonable grounds of federal criminal violations to the Attorney General [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal budget pays for the new offices (the bill sets minimum salaries of $225,000 for the chiefs and $180,000 for other counsels). The justices themselves give up part of their independence from outside scrutiny: their conduct becomes subject to staff review, required training, and congressional reporting.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers fund it; justices face scrutiny

drawbacks.text: The Chief Justice is only 'authorized' to establish the offices and appoints and can terminate the counsels — the entire structure sits inside the Court and depends on the Court's cooperation, so a Chief Justice could leave it dormant or staff it lightly [S2].

Only congressional leaders (the four Judiciary chairs and ranking members, the Senate leaders, and the House leaders) may file ethics complaints — an ordinary citizen, litigant, or journalist cannot trigger an investigation [S2].
The Chief Justice keeps sole discretion to release investigation reports to the public, so findings could remain permanently behind closed doors [S2].

Opponents argue Congress has limited power to impose structure on a coequal branch of government; the bill includes a severability clause anticipating that some provisions might be struck down as unconstitutional [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is modest — a handful of staff positions — and the accountability gain is real but partial: the design leaves the Chief Justice in charge of appointing, firing, and publicizing, which limits how independent the oversight can actually be. It is a meaningful first step toward formal ethics enforcement at the Court, not an independent watchdog.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Daniel Goldman introduced the bill on June 4, 2024, with 34 Democratic cosponsors, all members of the House [S2][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction; that was the last action ever recorded on it [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The sitting Supreme Court keeps its existing self-policing arrangement with no outside investigative staff, subpoena power, or congressional reporting. House Judiciary leadership avoided a vote on ethics oversight of the Court, and no member had to take a position on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Supreme Court, unchanged and self-policing

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on the day it was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 House supporters — the sponsor and 34 cosponsors — were Democrats, 34 of 216 House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-led Judiciary Committee took no action.

industries.industry: The Supreme Court and its nine justices
industries.note: The bill would end the Court's arrangement of policing itself without staff, subpoenas, or outside reporting, making justices subject to mandatory ethics training, complaint investigation, and annual congressional reports. For ordinary people, that is accountability for the most powerful judges in the country; for the justices, it is a real loss of autonomy.

industries.industry: Public-sector ethics staff and oversight attorneys
industries.note: The bill funds at least five senior legal positions (two chiefs at $225,000 and counsels at $180,000 minimum) inside the Court, creating a niche for ethics and investigative lawyers. The public gain only materializes if those staff actually produce independent oversight, which depends on the Chief Justice's cooperation.
